title: In Ezekiel 42 How Does The Separation Of The Outer Court From The Inner Sanctum Reflect The Holiness Of God
paragraphs: Understanding the Sacred Spaces in Ezekiel 42

Ezekiel 42 provides a detailed architectural description of the temple vision given to the prophet Ezekiel. This chapter specifically focuses on the chambers for the priests and the separation of different temple areas, especially the distinction between the outer court and the inner sanctum. This separation is not merely an architectural feature—rather, it is a profound theological statement about the holiness of God and the requirements for approaching His presence.
The Structure: A Brief Overview

Ezekiel describes “chambers for the priests” on both the north and south sides of the temple, adjacent to the separate place and the inner court (Ezekiel 42:1-14 ASV). These chambers are designated for the priests who minister in the sanctuary, and they serve as spaces for eating the most holy offerings and for storing sacred things.

Then said he unto me, The north chambers and the south chambers, which are before the separate place, they are the holy chambers, where the priests that are near unto Jehovah shall eat the most holy things: there shall they lay the most holy things, and the meal-offering, and the sin-offering, and the trespass-offering; for the place is holy. - Ezekiel 42:13 ASV
The Principle of Separation

The temple’s design—especially the clear separation between the outer court (where the people could come) and the inner sanctum (reserved for priests and the presence of God)—teaches us about God’s holiness. The inner sanctum, or “the holy place,” was not accessible to all. Only those consecrated for priestly service could enter, and even they had to follow strict rituals of purification.
This separation is emphasized in Ezekiel 42:20 ASV:

He measured it on the four sides: it had a wall round about, the length five hundred, and the breadth five hundred, to make a separation between that which was holy and that which was common. - Ezekiel 42:20 ASV
The Holiness of God

God’s holiness means He is utterly unique, morally pure, and set apart from all that is common or profane. The physical barriers in the temple serve as visible reminders that humans, in their sinfulness, cannot approach God casually or presumptuously. This echoes the broader biblical teaching:

Who shall ascend into the hill of Jehovah? And who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; Who hath not lifted up his soul unto falsehood, And hath not sworn deceitfully. - Psalm 24:3-4 ASV

The separation between holy and common space illustrates the necessity of purification, atonement, and a mediator for sinful people to come near to God. This is not because God is unapproachable, but because His holiness is overwhelming and incompatible with sin.
Christ: The Fulfillment of the Temple’s Separation

From a New Testament perspective, these temple separations point forward to the work of Jesus Christ. The curtain in the temple, which separated the Holy of Holies from the rest, was torn in two at the death of Jesus, signifying that access to God was now open to all who come through faith in Christ.

Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh. - Hebrews 10:19 ASV
Yet, the call to holiness remains. Those who trust in Christ are declared holy and are called to live set-apart lives in gratitude for God’s grace (1 Peter 1:15-16 ASV).
Application: Living in Light of God’s Holiness

Ezekiel 42’s attention to separation and purity challenges believers to revere God’s holiness and to approach Him with awe. While Christ has opened the way for intimate fellowship with God, we are still called to be holy, set apart from the world, as God is holy. This shapes how we worship, serve, and live daily.
Conclusion

The architectural separation in Ezekiel’s temple is a vivid illustration of God’s holiness and the requirements to approach Him. It finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who bridges the gap between sinful humanity and the Holy God, calling us to both reverence and relationship.
